title: The Bird That Silenced a Bullet Train

passage.title: The Bird That Silenced a Bullet Train
passage.author: DRC BEACON Assessment Passage
passage.text:
In the 1990s, rail engineers in Japan faced a loud problem as their bullet trains grew faster. These sleek trains glided between cities at nearly two hundred miles per hour. On open tracks, the ride was smooth and quiet. However, Japan is a land of steep hills. Its tracks pass through hundreds of narrow concrete tunnels. Every time a speeding train plunged into a tunnel mouth, a thunderous boom echoed out the far end.

The noise was so loud that it woke families living a quarter mile away from the tracks. The trouble came from physics inside the tight tube. Unlike air in an open field, the air trapped in a tunnel cannot slip past a blunt train nose. Pushed ahead like a solid wall at two hundred miles per hour, this trapped air was violently compressed by the flat front of the speeding train. When that squeezed wave of air burst out the exit, it cracked like a clap of thunder.

Fortunately, the chief engineer on the project, Eiji Nakatsu, was also an avid birdwatcher. He saw that the train was moving fast from thin open air into dense tunnel air. He asked himself what creature in nature dives smoothly from a thin medium into a much denser one. The answer was the kingfisher, a small river bird. It plunges from the air into water to catch fish and barely makes a ripple.

Nakatsu and his team tested the bird's shape in a wind tunnel. They saw that the kingfisher's beak is long, wedge-shaped, and tapered from a wide base to a sharp tip. Instead of shoving water forward, the bill parts the water evenly. It flows smoothly around the bird's head. The team reshaped the train's steel nose into a fifty-foot wedge modeled on that beak. During the next test run, the pressure wave dispersed harmlessly along the sides of the train, and the tunnel boom vanished.

The team also studied the silent wings of the owl to quiet the metal frames that collect power from wires above. An owl's wing feathers have tiny serrated edges, like the teeth on a comb, which break up noisy air swirls into soft micro-currents. By adding similar tiny grooves to the train's roof struts, engineers cut wind noise even more. Plus, the new train used fifteen percent less power while traveling even faster than before.

questions.prompt:
Read this sentence from Paragraph 2:

"Pushed ahead like a solid wall at two hundred miles per hour, this trapped air was violently compressed by the flat front of the speeding train."

Based on the structure of this sentence, what is performing the action of compressing?

options.text: The flat front of the speeding train
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 2, the passive verb 'was violently compressed by the flat front of the speeding train' tells us that the flat front of the speeding train performed the compressing.

options.text: The trapped air inside the narrow tunnel
options.childFeedback: The trapped air is what got squeezed ('this trapped air was violently compressed'), not the thing doing the squeezing.

options.text: A solid brick wall built across the tunnel exit
options.childFeedback: There was no brick wall across the tunnel; the author uses the simile 'like a solid wall' to describe how the pushed air piled up.

options.text: Families living a quarter mile away from the tracks
options.childFeedback: The families a quarter mile away only heard the loud boom after the compressed air wave burst out the tunnel exit.

questions.provingSentenceText: Pushed ahead like a solid wall at two hundred miles per hour, this trapped air was violently compressed by the flat front of the speeding train.
questions.childTip: In Paragraph 2, the passive verb 'was violently compressed by the flat front of the speeding train' tells us that the flat front of the speeding train performed the compressing.
questions.parentExplanation: In this passive-voice Monster Sentence, 'this trapped air' is the receiver of the action. The true actor squeezing the air is found in the prepositional agent phrase at the end: 'by the flat front of the speeding train' (Option A).
questions.retryHint: Look at the words right after 'compressed by' in the Paragraph 2 sentence to find what squeezed the trapped air.

questions.prompt:
Read this sentence from Paragraph 4:

"During the next test run, the pressure wave dispersed harmlessly along the sides of the train, and the tunnel boom vanished."

What does the word "dispersed" mean as it is used in this sentence?

options.text: Pushed the train backward to the previous city station
options.childFeedback: The pressure wave didn't push the bullet train backward; the train kept gliding forward while the air flowed smoothly along its sides.

options.text: Exploded with a louder boom at the mouth of the tunnel
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 4 says 'the tunnel boom vanished,' which is the exact opposite of exploding with a louder boom.

options.text: Froze into solid ice along the steel nose of the train
options.childFeedback: Nothing froze into ice in Paragraph 4; 'dispersed' describes how the air pressure spread out harmlessly along the sides of the train.

options.text: Spread out evenly instead of building up in one spot
options.childFeedback: In Paragraph 4, 'dispersed' means spread out evenly instead of building up in one spot, because the wedge-shaped nose parted the air smoothly along the sides so the boom vanished.

questions.provingSentenceText: During the next test run, the pressure wave dispersed harmlessly along the sides of the train, and the tunnel boom vanished.
questions.childTip: In Paragraph 4, 'dispersed' means spread out evenly instead of building up in one spot, because the wedge-shaped nose parted the air smoothly along the sides so the boom vanished.
questions.parentExplanation: In Paragraph 4, instead of packing into a compressed wall ahead of the train, the air parts around the wedge nose and spreads out ('dispersed harmlessly along the sides'), causing the boom to vanish (Option D).
questions.retryHint: Compare how the flat train nose shoved air into a tight wall in Paragraph 2 with how the wedge-shaped beak parted the air in Paragraph 4.

questions.prompt: Why did engineer Eiji Nakatsu study the kingfisher in Paragraph 3 to solve the bullet train's tunnel problem?

options.text: Kingfishers often build their nests inside concrete train tunnels in the Japanese mountains.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 3 calls the kingfisher 'a small river bird' that dives into water to catch fish, not a bird that nests inside concrete train tunnels.

options.text: Both the diving bird and the train entering a tunnel must move smoothly from thin air into a much denser space.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 3 explains that Nakatsu studied the kingfisher because just as the train moves fast from thin open air into dense tunnel air, the bird dives smoothly from thin air into dense water.

options.text: The kingfisher is the only bird on Earth that can fly at two hundred miles per hour.
options.childFeedback: The train travels at two hundred miles per hour, not the kingfisher; Nakatsu studied the shape of the bird's beak, not its flying speed.

options.text: The bird's wing feathers have serrated edges that collect electricity from overhead wires.
options.childFeedback: Owl wing feathers (not kingfisher feathers) have serrated edges in Paragraph 5, and real birds do not collect electricity from wires.

questions.provingSentenceText: He asked himself what creature in nature dives smoothly from a thin medium into a much denser one.
questions.childTip: Paragraph 3 explains that Nakatsu studied the kingfisher because just as the train moves fast from thin open air into dense tunnel air, the bird dives smoothly from thin air into dense water.
questions.parentExplanation: Paragraph 3 explains the analogy behind Nakatsu's insight: a train entering a tight tunnel shifts from thin open air to dense tunnel air, just as a kingfisher dives from thin air into dense water without making a splash (Option B).
questions.retryHint: Read the third and fourth sentences of Paragraph 3 to see what question Nakatsu asked himself about moving from a thin medium into a denser one.

questions.prompt: Which evidence from Paragraph 5 best supports the author's claim that copying bird designs improved more than just the train's noise level?

options.text: Eiji Nakatsu enjoyed watching river birds during his free time away from the rail yard.
options.childFeedback: Nakatsu's birdwatching hobby in Paragraph 3 explains how he got the idea, not how the finished train performed better in other ways besides noise.

options.text: The redesigned bullet train needed fifteen percent more electrical power and traveled slower than the older model.
options.childFeedback: This flips the facts in Paragraph 5: the redesigned train actually used fifteen percent LESS power and traveled FASTER than before.

options.text: The redesigned bullet train used fifteen percent less electrical power while traveling even faster than before.
options.childFeedback: The last sentence of Paragraph 5 proves that the bird-inspired designs did more than quiet the train: the new bullet train also used fifteen percent less power and traveled even faster.

options.text: Japanese tracks pass through hundreds of narrow concrete tunnels carved into steep mountains.
options.childFeedback: The concrete mountain tunnels are part of the setting and problem introduced in Paragraph 1, not an extra benefit of the bird-inspired redesign.

questions.provingSentenceText: Plus, the new train used fifteen percent less power while traveling even faster than before.
questions.childTip: The last sentence of Paragraph 5 proves that the bird-inspired designs did more than quiet the train: the new bullet train also used fifteen percent less power and traveled even faster.
questions.parentExplanation: Aligned to ELAGSE5RI8 (explaining how an author uses reasons and evidence to support particular points), the final sentence of Paragraph 5 proves that the biomimicry redesign also boosted energy efficiency ('fifteen percent less power') and speed (Option C).
questions.retryHint: Check the very last sentence of Paragraph 5 to see two extra benefits the redesigned train gained besides being quieter.

questions.prompt: PART A: How did the features copied from the kingfisher and the owl solve different parts of the bullet train's noise problem?

options.text: The kingfisher's wedge beak stopped air from piling up at the train's nose, while the owl's notched feather edges broke up wind swirls on the roof struts.
options.childFeedback: Paragraphs 4 and 5 show how the two birds solved two different noise sources: the kingfisher's wedge beak parted tunnel air at the nose, while the owl's serrated feather edges quieted air swirls on the roof struts.

options.text: The kingfisher's feathers quieted the train's wheels, while the owl's curved beak helped the train see inside dark mountain tunnels.
options.childFeedback: This mixes up both birds and parts! The kingfisher's beak (not feathers) shaped the train's steel nose, and the owl's feathers (not beak) quieted the roof struts.

options.text: Both birds taught engineers how to build wider concrete tunnels so air waves would never touch the sides of the train.
options.childFeedback: Engineers reshaped the train's nose and roof struts rather than rebuilding hundreds of mountain tunnels across Japan.

options.text: The kingfisher design made the train slower in tunnels, while the owl design turned off the overhead power wires completely.
options.childFeedback: Paragraph 5 states that the new train traveled even faster and still collected power from overhead wires using the grooved roof struts.

questions.provingSentenceText: An owl's wing feathers have tiny serrated edges, like the teeth on a comb, which break up noisy air swirls into soft micro-currents.
questions.childTip: Paragraphs 4 and 5 show how the two birds solved two different noise sources: the kingfisher's wedge beak parted tunnel air at the nose, while the owl's serrated feather edges quieted air swirls on the roof struts.
questions.parentExplanation: Synthesizing Paragraphs 4 and 5 shows that the kingfisher's wedge-shaped beak parted tunnel air at the nose (Paragraph 4), whereas the owl's serrated feather edges inspired grooves on the roof struts to break up noisy wind swirls (Paragraph 5, Option A). Option B swaps the two birds' traits.
questions.retryHint: Compare what part of the train copied the kingfisher's beak in Paragraph 4 with what part copied the owl's feathers in Paragraph 5.

questions.prompt: PART B: Which quotation from the passage best supports the correct answer to Question 5?

options.text: "Every time a speeding train plunged into a tunnel mouth, a thunderous boom echoed out the far end."
options.childFeedback: This sentence from Paragraph 1 only describes the original tunnel boom problem, before engineers studied either the kingfisher or the owl.

options.text: "Fortunately, the chief engineer on the project, Eiji Nakatsu, was also an avid birdwatcher."
options.childFeedback: This line from Paragraph 3 tells us that Nakatsu liked birdwatching, without explaining how the bird features actually stopped the noise.

options.text: "An owl's wing feathers have tiny serrated edges, like the teeth on a comb, which break up noisy air swirls into soft micro-currents."
options.childFeedback: This quotation from Paragraph 5 directly supports Question 5 by explaining how the owl's serrated feather edges break up noisy air swirls into soft micro-currents.

options.text: "The noise was so loud that it woke families living a quarter mile away from the tracks."
options.childFeedback: This detail from Paragraph 2 shows how loud the old train was for nearby families, rather than showing how the kingfisher or owl features solved the problem.

questions.provingSentenceText: An owl's wing feathers have tiny serrated edges, like the teeth on a comb, which break up noisy air swirls into soft micro-currents.
questions.childTip: This quotation from Paragraph 5 directly supports Question 5 by explaining how the owl's serrated feather edges break up noisy air swirls into soft micro-currents.
questions.parentExplanation: Option C directly proves the mechanism described in Part A by quoting how the owl's serrated edges break noisy air swirls into soft micro-currents.
questions.retryHint: Look for the quote from Paragraph 5 that explains how the owl's notched feather edges stop noisy air swirls.
